title: Deepfakes & Misinformation
hook: Seeing is no longer believing. AI can now fake a photo, a voice, or a video convincingly enough to fool a quick glance — so the new skill is knowing when to doubt.
key_points: Deepfakes are AI-made fake images, audio, or video of real people.
They're getting cheaper, faster, and harder to spot by eye.
Used for scams, fake news, and harassment — context matters more than visuals.
Best defense: check the source, look for confirmation, and pause before sharing.
content_html: For most of history, a photo or a recording was strong evidence that something really happened. AI is ending that assumption. Deepfakes — synthetic images, audio, and video generated by AI — can now put words in a politician's mouth, clone a relative's voice on a phone call, or fabricate an event that never took place. The technology is improving fast and getting cheaper, so the old tell-tale signs (weird hands, off-sync lips) are disappearing.
extra_html: Because you increasingly can't spot a fake by looking harder, the useful skill shifts from "examine the pixels" to "examine the source." Where did this come from? Is a credible outlet reporting it? Does anything confirm it independently, or is it a single dramatic clip designed to be shared? Scammers use voice clones to fake emergencies ("Mom, I'm in trouble, send money"); bad actors use fake videos to spread misinformation, especially around elections. The practical habits are simple but powerful: be skeptical of emotionally charged media from unknown sources, verify before you believe, and pause before you share — sharing is how misinformation travels.

related.title: AI Images, Art & Video
related.hook: Type a sentence, get a picture. Image generators learned the link between words and visuals from billions of captioned images — which is also why artists are raising hard questions.

related.title: AI Scams & Staying Safe
related.hook: AI didn't invent scams — it just made them cheaper, faster, and far more convincing. The good news: the habits that beat them haven't changed.

flashcards.explanation_html: Deepfakes use AI to synthesize convincing fake media — a face, a voice, a whole video — of someone, often saying or doing things they never did.

flashcards.prompt: What's the most reliable way to judge a suspicious clip?
flashcards.back_html: Check the source and look for independent confirmation, rather than trusting your eyes — and pause before sharing.
